```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  collapse = TRUE,
  comment = "#>"
)

library("conquestr")
```

_conquestr_ has three main functions: 

- ConQuestCall: calls 'ACER ConQuest' in a terminal and runs syntax
- ConQuestSys: reads and returns 'ACER ConQuest' system files as an R object. For example, this provides access to parameter estimates, abilities, and raw data. 
- ConQuestRout (and plotRout): reads 'ACER ConQuest' plot objects (see the command [plot](https://conquestmanual.acer.org/s4-00.html#plot)) and creates plots in R via generic functions and dispatch.

These functions allows users to include 'ACER ConQuest' within their R workflow. This is particularly useful for users of the Mac OS X version (and Windows console) version of 'ACER ConQuest' which does not support ploting.

This vignette demonstrates how to use the package built-in demonstration files to:

- Call 'ACER ConQuest' and run a syntax file
- Read in a system file and access data objects

## Call ConQuest and run a syntax file

First, ensure you have the most current version of ConQuest. Version > 5.17.4 is required. If you are unsure, check [ConQuest on the ACER Shop](https://shop.acer.org/collections/acer-conquest-5).
You will also need to install the conquestr library:

```
install.packages("conquestr")
library("conquestr")
```

You must pass the `ConQuestCall` function at least two pieces of information: the install location of ConQuest and a valid syntax file.
_conquestr_ has included syntax files that can be used to run a model and test other package functions. 
A default syntax file will be called is you do not explicitly provide one. 
_conquestr_ will search for a valid installation of 'ACER ConQuest' unless the executable is explicitly declared.
The search locations are (in order): 

- The default install location (Windows:`%ProgramFiles%\ACER ConQuest\ConQuestConsole.exe` and Mac OS X: `/Applications/ConQuest/ConQuest`).
- The Program Files folder on Windows, and the Application folder on Mac OS X
- The current user's Desktop

```
# if you don't provide a syntax file, using the argumenmt `cqc=`, then the in-built demo syntax file will be run. 
ConQuestCall() 

```

```
# the following output is produced:

ConQuest build: Mar 10 2021
<TYPE> Version
This version expires <DATE>
submit <PATH>conquestr/extdata/conquestabout.cqc;
=>dir;
<PATH>
=>about;
Developed by
    Australian Council for Educational Research
    University of California,Berkeley

<TYPE> Build:  <DATE>

```

When you use `ConQuestCall` to call 'ACER ConQuest' and run a syntax file, some options are set by default. The same options can be set within 'ACER ConQuest' by using the `set` command (`set progress = yes, exit_on_error = yes, storecommands = yes, warnings = no;` which is syntactically the same as using the helper function `set conquestr = true;`). **WARNING** - this will make it easy to overwrite output as you will not be prompted or warned. To turn off these settings your syntax file must explicitly change these using the `set` command. 
For more information see [the set command](https://conquestmanual.acer.org/s4-00.html#set).

When calling 'ACER ConQuest' from R, the ConQuest working directory will default to the current R working directory. This makes it easy to write portable syntax using relative paths. If you need 'ACER ConQuest' to use a different working directory, set it in your syntax file.

The next example runs a small analysis and creates a system file that is read into the R object `myExSys`.

```{r}
# set up
oldWd <- getwd()
myTmpDir <- tempdir()
setwd(myTmpDir)
file.copy(from = c(
  system.file("extdata", "ex1.cqc", package = "conquestr"),
  system.file("extdata", "ex1.dat", package = "conquestr"),
  system.file("extdata", "mysysfile.cqs", package = "conquestr")
  ), to = myTmpDir)

# run ConQuest
# ConQuestCall is not run here, as it requires a local install of ConQuest 
# ConQuestCall(cqc = file.path(myTmpDir, "ex1.cqc"), stdout = NULL) # searches for valid install of CQ
myExSys <- ConQuestSys(myCqs = file.path(myTmpDir, "mysysfile.cqs"))

# see the content of the sysfile
str(myExSys)

# tidy up
file.remove(
  list.files(myTmpDir, all.files = TRUE, full.names = TRUE, pattern = "^myi|^myS|ex1"),
  recursive=TRUE
)
setwd(oldWd)
```

## Read in a ConQuest system file

The above example created a system file. Alternatively, there is an inbuilt example of a system file.

_conquestr_ can read in a system file, using the `ConQuestSys` function. This function returns a list that includes the response data, parameter estimates, and other data objects created by 'ACER ConQuest'. These lists can be optionally coerced into R data frames.

```{r}
# if no argument is provided to ConQuestSys, the example system file is read in by default.
myCqs <- ConQuestSys()
```

You can see the data objects available within the object (e.g., `str(myCqs)`), and some useful objects will be:

- `gResponseData` - The raw response data including information about the raw and key response to each item.
- `gYData` - The regression data included in the estimation.
- `gAllCaseEstimates` - the latent ability estimates (e.g., PVs, WLEs).
- The option `matrixout` is available for several commands and will ensure data objects are saved to the system file - these can be found in `gMatrixList`. For example:
    - The command `matrixsampler` and the option `matrixout` creates the objects `matrixSampler_fit`, `matrixSampler_raw`, `matrix_userfit` (the simulated data) in `gMatrixList`.
    - The command `itanal`, and the option `matrixout` creates the objects `*_counts`, `*_itemstats`, `*_ptbis`, `*_abilitymeansd` (where "*" is a user defined prefix declared in the  option `matrixout`) in `gMatrixList` .
    - The command `estimate` and the option `matrixout`... for more information see the [manual](https://conquestmanual.acer.org/s4-00.html#s4-08)

Users can search the names of objects in the system file using the helper function `searchConQuestSys`:

```{r}
# search for objects named history in myCqs
searchConQuestSys("history", myCqs)
```



## Population statistics from plausible values

Large-scale assessments such as PISA report student achievement as a set of
plausible values (PVs) and provide replicate weights for estimating sampling
error. `conquestr` provides a family of functions that compute a statistic for
each PV under the full-sample weight and under every replicate weight, then
combine the results using Rubin's rules:

- `pvStat()` - the core function (any supported statistic, optionally by group)
- `pvMean()`, `pvSd()`, `pvVar()`, `pvMedian()`, `pvQuantile()`, `pvIqr()` and `pvDescribe()`
- `pvDiff()` - differences between groups (e.g., girls minus boys)
- `pvCor()` - correlations between PVs and background variables
- `pvRegression()` - weighted linear regression of PVs on background variables

Supported replication methods are `"BRR"`, `"Fay"` (Fay's variant of BRR, as
used in PISA), `"JK1"` (delete-one jackknife) and `"JK2"` (paired jackknife, as
used in TIMSS and PIRLS).

### Simulate a PISA-style dataset

The example below simulates 64 schools in 32 variance strata (pairs of
schools), 20 students per school, 10 PVs and Fay replicate weights
(`k = 0.5`) built from a Hadamard matrix. PISA uses 80 replicates; 32 are used
here to keep the example small.

```{r pv-sim}
set.seed(5309)
nStrata <- 32
nSchools <- nStrata * 2
nPerSchool <- 20
nPVs <- 10

# Sylvester construction of a 32 x 32 Hadamard matrix
hadamard <- matrix(1)
while (nrow(hadamard) < nStrata) hadamard <- rbind(cbind(hadamard, hadamard), cbind(hadamard, -hadamard))

school <- rep(seq_len(nSchools), each = nPerSchool)
stratum <- (school + 1) %/% 2
unit <- ifelse(school %% 2 == 1, 1, -1) # first or second school in the pair
n <- length(school)

pisaSim <- data.frame(
  school = school,
  sex = factor(sample(c("boy", "girl"), n, replace = TRUE)),
  escs = rnorm(nSchools, 0, 0.5)[school] + rnorm(n, 0, 0.8),
  W_FSTUWT = runif(n, 5, 50)
)
schoolEffect <- rnorm(nSchools, 0, 40)[school]
trueTheta <- 480 + 30 * pisaSim$escs + 12 * (pisaSim$sex == "girl") + schoolEffect + rnorm(n, 0, 70)
for (p in seq_len(nPVs)) {
  pisaSim[[paste0("PV", p, "READ")]] <- trueTheta + rnorm(n, 0, 25) # imputation noise
}

# Fay replicate weights: one school in each pair gets 1.5, the other 0.5
fayK <- 0.5
for (r in seq_len(nStrata)) {
  factorR <- ifelse(hadamard[stratum, r] * unit > 0, 2 - fayK, fayK)
  pisaSim[[paste0("W_FSTR", r)]] <- pisaSim$W_FSTUWT * factorR
}

pvs <- paste0("PV", seq_len(nPVs), "READ")
repWts <- paste0("W_FSTR", seq_len(nStrata))
```

### Descriptive statistics

`pvDescribe()` returns the mean, SD, variance, quartiles and IQR. Each row
reports the estimate, its standard error (`se`), the sampling variance U
(`samplingVar`) and the between-PV variance B (`imputationVar`).

```{r pv-describe}
pvDescribe(pisaSim, pvs, weight = "W_FSTUWT", repWeights = repWts,
           repMethod = "Fay", fayK = fayK, by = "sex")
```

`imputationVar` is B *before* Rubin's correction, so the columns do not
simply add up to `se^2`. The reported estimate is the average of only M PV
estimates, and that average has its own simulation error with variance B / M.
Rubin's rules add it, so the total error variance is

$$\mathrm{SE}^2 = U + \left(1 + \tfrac{1}{M}\right) B.$$

With 10 PVs this adds 10% to B. To recover `se` from the columns:

```{r pv-se-check}
desc <- pvDescribe(pisaSim, pvs, weight = "W_FSTUWT", repWeights = repWts,
                   repMethod = "Fay", fayK = fayK)
all.equal(desc$se, sqrt(desc$samplingVar + (1 + 1 / desc$nPVs) * desc$imputationVar))
```

The same holds for `pvDiff()`, `pvCor()` (on the z scale when
`combine = "fisherZ"`) and `pvRegression()`. See `?pvStat` for details.

### Group differences

`pvDiff()` computes the difference within each PV and replicate, so the
standard error accounts for the covariance between groups that is induced by
the sampling design.

```{r pv-diff}
pvDiff(pisaSim, pvs, by = "sex", pairs = list(c("girl", "boy")),
       weight = "W_FSTUWT", repWeights = repWts, repMethod = "Fay", fayK = fayK)
```

### Correlations

`pvCor()` combines correlations on the raw r scale by default, or on the
Fisher-z scale with `combine = "fisherZ"`. The Fisher-z option gives
confidence intervals that stay within [-1, 1].

```{r pv-cor}
pvCor(pisaSim, pvs, "escs", weight = "W_FSTUWT", repWeights = repWts,
      repMethod = "Fay", fayK = fayK, combine = "fisherZ")
```

### Regression

`pvRegression()` takes a one-sided formula of predictors; the PVs are the
outcome.

```{r pv-reg}
pvRegression(pisaSim, pvs, ~ escs + sex, weight = "W_FSTUWT",
             repWeights = repWts, repMethod = "Fay", fayK = fayK)
```

### Correlation and covariance matrices

`pvCorMatrix()` and `pvCovMatrix()` estimate the matrix for several
measures at once. Each measure is either latent (its PV columns, in draw
order) or manifest (a single observed column). Latent measures are paired by
draw (PV1 with PV1, PV2 with PV2, ...), which is appropriate when their PVs
were drawn jointly from one multidimensional model. A manifest variable is
the same in every draw, so its column is reused for each PV.

To illustrate, add a second latent domain (mathematics) drawn jointly with
reading, and an observed variable (age in months):

```{r pv-sim-md}
trueMath <- 0.7 * (trueTheta - 480) + 470 + rnorm(n, 0, 60)
for (p in seq_len(nPVs)) {
  shared <- rnorm(n) # joint draw: reading and maths PV p share an error component
  pisaSim[[paste0("PV", p, "MATH")]] <- trueMath + 20 * shared + rnorm(n, 0, 15)
}
pisaSim$age <- round(rnorm(n, 189, 3.5))

measures <- list(
  read = paste0("PV", seq_len(nPVs), "READ"),
  math = paste0("PV", seq_len(nPVs), "MATH"),
  escs = "escs",
  age = "age"
)
```

The matrix format returns symmetric matrices of estimates, standard errors
and confidence limits:

```{r pv-cormat}
corMat <- pvCorMatrix(pisaSim, measures, weight = "W_FSTUWT", repWeights = repWts,
                      repMethod = "Fay", fayK = fayK, format = "matrix")
round(corMat$estimate, 3)
round(corMat$se, 3)
```

The long format has one row per pair. Pairs of two manifest variables are
ordinary weighted correlations, so `imputationVar` is 0 and `nPVs` is 1:

```{r pv-cormat-long}
pvCorMatrix(pisaSim, measures, weight = "W_FSTUWT", repWeights = repWts,
            repMethod = "Fay", fayK = fayK)[, c("dim1", "dim2", "estimate", "se",
                                                 "imputationVar", "nPVs")]
```

`pvCovMatrix()` returns variances on the diagonal; these match `pvVar()`:

```{r pv-covmat}
covMat <- pvCovMatrix(pisaSim, measures, weight = "W_FSTUWT", repWeights = repWts,
                      repMethod = "Fay", fayK = fayK, format = "matrix")
round(covMat$estimate, 1)
pvVar(pisaSim, measures$read, weight = "W_FSTUWT", repWeights = repWts,
      repMethod = "Fay", fayK = fayK)$estimate
```

Two cautions apply when mixing latent and manifest measures:

- A correlation between PVs and an observed variable is unbiased only if
  that variable (or a good proxy) was in the population (conditioning) model
  used to draw the PVs; otherwise it is biased towards zero. Here `age` was
  not used to generate the PVs and is unrelated to proficiency, so its
  correlations are near zero by construction. Check the study's scaling
  documentation before interpreting such correlations.
- With `combine = "fisherZ"`, each element is back-transformed separately,
  so the matrix is not guaranteed to be positive semi-definite; a warning is
  given if it is not. The default, `combine = "raw"`, always gives a valid
  matrix.
